transcript:
Meeting header: 
Date: 2025-02-14
Start time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Reyes, Samira Patel, Liam O'Neil, Alex Chen, Priya Rao

Summary: Initial technical screen for frontend SWE role. Live-coding prompt (small component), discussion on perf tradeoffs, testing and monitoring.

Transcript body:
00:00 Jordan: Hey Alex, thanks for making time, we showed up on calendar at 3pm, is now still good?
00:08 Alex: Yep yep, all good. Thanks for having me, excited to chat.
00:15 Liam: quick intro, I'm Liam from recruiting, I'll hand off to Jordan and Samira for the technical part.
00:25 Jordan: great. We'll do ~45 minutes tech + 5-10 for logistics. Samira is going to lead the live-coding.
00:35 Samira: Hi Alex. Can you tell us briefly about the last frontend project you worked on, especially any perf issues you had to solve?
00:45 Alex: Sure. At NeoCloud Labs I built a dashboard that started to slow down when lists grew past 2k items. We introduced virtualization with react-window, memoized expensive renderers, and added incremental loading. We also shipped an observer-based lazy loading for images and saw CPU drop by ~30%.
01:10 Jordan: nice. When you say memoized renderers, were you using pure components, useMemo, or something else? Did you measure the win?
01:20 Alex: mostly useMemo and React.memo. We profiled with Chrome devtools flame charts and a custom trace that logged render durations; removed deep object props to avoid unnecessary memo invalidation. It was a combination of app-level fixes and some server-side pagination too.
01:45 Samira: follow-up: how would you approach a situation where virtualization gives unexpected UX issues like scroll jumps when filters change?
01:55 Alex: I'd implement stable keys, avoid re-creating list items on filter change, maybe keep an index map. If items change size, we'd consider a dynamic virtualization strategy or measure heights and buffer around viewport. Also communicate to product if filters need server-side re-aggregation.
02:30 Jordan: shifting gears, we want to hear your thoughts on component testing vs end-to-end for a complex dashboard. What has worked?
02:40 Alex: unit tests for core logic and snapshot for simple render shapes, but rely on a few e2e flows for user journeys. Use MSW to mock APIs for deterministic tests. Emphasize quick feedback loops in CI and keep e2e as a guardrail to catch integration regressions.
03:10 Samira: live-coding: build a small React component that renders a list of items with a search input. It should debounce input and show match count. You can pseudocode; focus on approach.
03:25 Alex: okay, I'll outline. useState for query, useEffect with setTimeout for debounce, or useCallback with lodash debounce. For match count, filter items by normalized text, memoize filtered result with useMemo. Avoid filtering on every keystroke by debouncing.
04:10 Alex: (typing) const [q, setQ] = useState(''); const debouncedQ = useDebounce(q, 200); const filtered = useMemo(() => items.filter(...), [items, debouncedQ]); return (...)
04:50 Samira: interruption: do you prefer custom hooks for debounce or utility libs?
04:55 Alex: pref lib for reliability, but custom hook is fine if small; ensure cleanup to avoid leaks.
05:20 Jordan: any pitfalls you want to call out?
05:25 Alex: accessibility — ensure input labeled, announce counts for screen readers, keyboard nav between results. Also consider pagination for very large datasets.
06:00 Samira: quick follow: how would you instrument performance for this component in prod?
06:10 Alex: add RUM metrics around input latency, measure render times with PerformanceObserver or user timing marks, sample sessions to see event frequency, track debounce delays, and tie to error logs. Use feature flags to roll out heavier instrumentation.
06:40 Jordan: good. A couple of scenario questions: if switching to server-side search because of large payloads, how would you design the API and client?
06:50 Alex: design paginated API with search query and cursor; client would show loading state, optimistic placeholder rows; cancel inflight requests on new queries; use abort controllers. Also cache recent queries for quick back/forward UX.
07:30 Samira: hands-on debugging question: you deploy a change and see a 10% increase in main-thread time for the dashboard. How do you triage?
07:40 Alex: reproduce with profiler, compare flame charts pre/post, identify hot components, check network waterfall for larger payloads, verify bundle size changes, source-map to identify new code, and roll back if necessary.
08:10 Jordan: do you have experience with code-splitting or lazy loading routes?
08:15 Alex: yes — route-based code-splitting with React.lazy and Suspense, chunk naming, prefetching critical chunks. Monitor TTFB and LCP; use lifecycle hooks to prefetch on hover for links.
09:00 Samira: behavioral: tell us about a time you had to push back on product about a feature due date because of technical debt.
09:10 Alex: described a time where we delayed a release to refactor a shared renderer; presented quantifiable risks and a mitigation plan; product accepted a smaller MVP and a follow-up iteration.
09:40 Jordan: wrap technical — overall impressions: strong on pragmatic trade-offs, good observability instincts. Recruiter will cover logistics next.
09:55 Liam: logistics: compensation bands, notice period? Also next steps.
10:05 Alex: notice is two weeks, currently IC at NeoCloud Labs, open to relocation but prefer remote-first.
10:20 Liam: thanks. We'll ask you to complete a small take-home to validate an implementation and tests. Expect an email with details.
10:35 Priya: (recruiter) quick clarifying Q: are you currently on any non-competes?
10:40 Alex: no.
10:45 Jordan: final: is there anything you'd like to ask us about the role or team?
10:50 Alex: asked about team size, on-call expectations, career growth. Samira answered that the frontend org is 6 engineers, shared on-call for infra, focus on building reusable components.
11:20 Jordan: thanks Alex. We'll wrap up. Liam will follow up with next steps.
11:30 Meeting end.

Notes: Transcript contains natural speech patterns and brief interruptions. Some technical terms abbreviated; occasional filler words removed for readability.
